captions.instagram:
How does the nose smell?

Your nose is two 10 cm tunnels with a stamp-sized smell patch in the roof, about 400 kinds of receptor, and a direct line to the brain's memory centres. Sniff air up to the patch, watch molecules fit their receptors, and see why a mango is mostly smell.

→ Behind your nose are two 10 cm tunnels, split by a wall called the septum.
→ Only a stamp-sized patch high in the roof can smell. A sniff sends air up to it.
→ Freezing air in, warm wet air out: the nose heats each breath to about 30 °C in a fraction of a second.
→ Every few hours your two nostrils swap: one swells while the other opens.
→ Smell molecules drift up into the mucus and fit receptors on tiny hairs. Each fit fires a neuron.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox.how/noseclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: How does the nose smell? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
Your nose is two 10 cm tunnels with a stamp-sized smell patch in the roof, about 400 kinds of receptor, and a direct line to the brain's memory centres. Sniff air up to the patch, watch molecules fit their receptors, and see why a mango is mostly smell.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox.how/e/noseclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/noseclear

In this video:
• Two tunnels and a smell patch. Behind your nostrils, two nasal cavities run about 10 cm back, split by the septum.
• A built-in air conditioner. The turbinates are warm, wet and full of blood vessels.
• About 400 locks, endless barcodes. Smell molecules dissolve in the mucus and fit receptors on the cilia of millions of smell neurons.
• A short cut into the brain. Neurons with the same receptor all wire to the same glomeruli in the olfactory bulb.
• Flavour is mostly smell. The tongue senses five basic tastes.
• When smell goes wrong. Colds block air from the smell patch, COVID-19 took smell from roughly 40 to 50% of patients early in the pandemic, and smell fades with age.
